content:
It is probable that Śiva's worship in the form of liṅga had not yet come into vogue when Patañjali wrote his great commentary on Pāṇini. The bronze seal belonging to the first century B.C. found at Sirkāp site (Taxila) by John Marśal carries an iconic representation of Śiva, along with the legend 'Śiva-rakṣita' ("protected by Śiva") in Brāhmi and Kharōṣṭhī characters.
By the time the Gupta empire was formed (around 320 A.D.). The Śaiva religion had already become crystallized. One of the monarchs of this dynasty, Vainya-gupta, is recorded to have been a 'great devotee of Śiva'. The earliest mukha-liṅga (representation of Śiva in a liṅga but with the human face of Śiva carved in it) which was found at Khoh, belongs to the early Gupta period. The Vākāṭaka rulers (275-550 A.D.) Styled themselves with such titles as 'atyanta-māheśvara' and 'atyanta-svāmi-mahā-bhairava-bhakta', which indicate their zeal for the worship of siva. Even the Ephthalite chieftain, Mihira-gula (515-535 A.D.) was a worshipper of Śiva as Paśupati. His coins bear a representation of bull as Śiva's insignia, with the legend "May victorious be the Bull". The kings of the North who wielded great influence after the Guptas, viz. the Maukharis, were also 'parama-māheśvaras'.
There is a suggestion that worship of Śiva was indigenous to South India. But it seems probable that Śaivism as a sect was first organized in Central India, and that it subsequently spread to Kāśmīr and South India.
From the eighth to the twelth century A.D., Śaivism prevailed in Madhyapradesha, Kānya'ubja, Gujarat, Lāṭa and Kāśmīra. The major factor that moved the focus of Śaivism from Central India to Kāśmīra and South India was the uncertain political conditions in Central India.
summary: This text traces the historical development of Śaivism in India. It suggests that liṅga worship was not prevalent in Patañjali's time, but iconic representations of Śiva existed by the first century B.C., as evidenced by a seal from Taxila. By the Gupta period (c. 320 A.D.), Śaivism was well-established, with patronage from rulers like Vainya-gupta, the Vākāṭakas, the Ephthalite chief Mihira-gula, and the Maukharis. The text addresses the origin of the sect, arguing it was likely organized first in Central India before spreading to Kāśmīr and South India. This spread, particularly between the 8th and 12th centuries A.D., was significantly influenced by political instability in Central India.
key_themes: Development of Śaiva iconography (iconic representation, liṅga, mukha-liṅga)
Royal patronage of Śaivism across various dynasties
Geographical origins and spread of the Śaiva sect
main_arguments: The worship of Śiva in the form of the liṅga is a later development, not present during the time of Patañjali.
Śaivism as a formal religion was crystallized and widely supported by various ruling dynasties by the Gupta period.
Contrary to suggestions of a South Indian origin, it is more probable that Śaivism as an organized sect originated in Central India.
The shift of Śaivism's focus from Central India to Kāśmīra and South India was driven by political instability in the former region.
methodology: The methodology is historical and archaeological, relying on a synthesis of evidence from multiple sources. This includes textual analysis (Patañjali's commentary on Pāṇini), archaeological artifacts (a bronze seal from Taxila discovered by John Marśal), iconographic evidence (the earliest mukha-liṅga from Khoh), numismatics (coins of Mihira-gula), and epigraphy (royal titles such as 'atyanta-māheśvara'). The author uses this evidence to construct a chronological and geographical narrative of Śaivism's development.
historiographical_context: The text engages with a specific historiographical debate concerning the origins of organized Śaivism. It acknowledges the "suggestion that worship of Śiva was indigenous to South India" but presents a counter-argument, favoring a Central Indian origin. This positions the work within the broader scholarly discussion on the regional origins and transmission of major religious sects in ancient and medieval India. It also builds upon the foundational archaeological work of figures like John Marśal.
research_questions: What is the chronological development of Śiva worship and its iconography, particularly the liṅga, in ancient India?
What evidence exists for royal patronage of Śaivism in the post-Mauryan and Gupta periods?
Where did Śaivism as an organized sect originate, and what were the patterns of its subsequent geographical spread?
What political or social factors contributed to the shifting centers of Śaivism from Central India to other regions like Kāśmīra and South India?
